title: Sask. man talked about suicide before being killed in shootout with police, says wife
article: A man talked about suicide just hours before he was shot to death in a harrowing confrontation with Saskatoon police, his wife told an inquest Monday.
Just hours before he led police on a high- speed chase on May 20, 2001, Keldon McMillan told his wife Kim Clayton it was time for him to end his life.
"He indicated that I would be the one carrying the guilt for that," Clayton testified.
Clayton said she decided to leave her husband on May 18, after a nasty fight in front of their three-year-old daughter.
She said she recently had learned they were going to lose their newly built home in northeast Saskatoon and financial problems with her husband's business were more severe than he would admit.
She decided to take their daughter to spend the long weekend at friends. McMillan called the home looking for her at about 2 a.m., then came over to try to convince her to come home.
When she refused and the argument became heated, she went to call 911.
"I heard him say that if I called the police somebody was going to die ... he said that if the police came there was going to be a shootout," Clayton said.
The next evening, police were called to the couple's new home. As they pulled up, McMillan drove his truck out of the garage and cut through the unfinished yard onto an adjoining street.

Three city police cruisers followed onto Highway 41. McMillan avoided one RCMP spike belt during the high-speed chase that followed over the next 80 kilometres, but a second one flattened three of his tires.

Saskatoon police Const. Kenneth King testified McMillan got out of his truck and fired his handgun once into the air almost immediately after he came to a stop several metres from the road's edge, then began walking along the side of a field.
Three city police officers were along the highway's edge, weapons drawn. McMillan ignored repeated commands to drop his gun, so a police dog was ordered to attack, King said.
McMillan shot the dog twice, but the dog still managed to bite him on RCMP officers at the scene fired their weapons.
McMillan was only hit by the shotgun blasts and it left eight pellets in his chest, pelvis and one leg.
He died within minutes, the inquest heard.

A six-member coroner's jury is expected to rule on the time, place and cause of death, and may make recommendations on how to prevent similar tragedies, but they may not assign civil or criminal blame.
